def: Excessive, involuntary or purposeless movement, as in chorea, tics, tremor or restless hyperactivity. Seen in basal ganglia disorders such as Huntington disease.
Benign hereditary reduction of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity causing mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Jaundice appears with fasting, illness or stress; no treatment is needed.
Perisinusoidal cells in the space of Disse that store vitamin A. When activated by liver injury they make collagen, driving hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis.
An oral iron chelator used for transfusional iron overload in thalassemia and sickle cell disease. Can cause agranulocytosis.
Arteries along the greater curvature of the stomach: the right arises from the gastroduodenal artery and the left from the splenic artery; they anastomose with each other.
The duct formed by the union of the right and left hepatic ducts; it joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct.
Specialized epithelial cells overlying Peyer patches in the gut that sample luminal antigens and pass them to underlying immune cells. Also called microfold cells.
The generation of vast numbers of different antibodies by V(D)J recombination, junctional diversity, somatic hypermutation and heavy and light chain pairing.

Failure to mount an immune response against self or harmless antigens, achieved by clonal deletion (central tolerance) and anergy or regulatory T cells (peripheral tolerance). Loss causes autoimmunity.
A formaldehyde-inactivated diphtheria toxin used as a vaccine antigen (DTaP, Tdap); it induces antibodies that neutralize the toxin.
An inactivated vaccine given before or after exposure to rabies virus, always combined after exposure with rabies immune globulin because the disease has a long incubation period.
A localized type III hypersensitivity reaction in which injected antigen forms immune complexes with preexisting IgG in the skin, causing edema, hemorrhage and necrosis within hours.
Tissue transplanted from one site to another in the same individual, so no rejection occurs.
Tissue transplanted between different species, such as porcine heart valves. Subject to hyperacute rejection.
A graft between genetically identical individuals, such as identical twins; no rejection occurs.
Fibrotic narrowing and obstruction of the small airways, causing progressive dyspnea with an obstructive pattern. Seen after lung or bone marrow transplant (chronic rejection) and toxic inhalations.
Conserved microbial molecules (such as LPS, flagellin, peptidoglycan and unmethylated CpG DNA) recognized by innate immune pattern recognition receptors like Toll-like receptors.
The most reactive reactive oxygen species, formed from hydrogen peroxide and Fe2+ (Fenton reaction), damaging DNA, lipids and proteins.
An immunoglobulin-family adhesion molecule on endothelium induced by inflammation. It binds LFA-1 on leukocytes, enabling firm adhesion before transmigration.
An endothelial adhesion molecule induced by cytokines that binds VLA-4 on leukocytes, helping them adhere and migrate into tissue.
A chemokine (CXCL8) from macrophages and endothelium that attracts neutrophils to sites of inflammation.
A bleach-like oxidant produced by myeloperoxidase from hydrogen peroxide and chloride in neutrophil phagolysosomes; kills ingested microbes.
A gram-negative rod found in water and soil that causes difficult-to-treat lung infections in cystic fibrosis and chronic granulomatous disease patients.
A dye reduced by phagocyte oxidative burst to a dark blue color; the test is negative (no color change) in chronic granulomatous disease. Dihydrorhodamine testing has replaced it.
An iron-binding protein in neutrophil granules, milk, tears and mucosal secretions that limits bacterial growth by sequestering iron.

Inherited lack of complement proteins. C1 to C4 deficiency causes immune complex disease (lupus-like); C5 to C9 deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria infections; C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema.
Systemic sclerosis with skin thickening extending proximal to the elbows and knees and trunk. Associated with anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) antibodies and early lung and kidney involvement.
The most common cartilage, with a glassy matrix of type II collagen; found in articular surfaces, the trachea, nose and the embryonic skeleton (including growth plates).
The shaft of a long bone, made of compact bone around the medullary cavity.
A benign tumor of hyaline cartilage within the medullary cavity, usually in the small bones of the hand. Multiple enchondromas occur in Ollier disease.
Autoantibodies against proteins in which arginine is converted to citrulline; highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis, often present before symptoms appear.
The postsynaptic region of a skeletal muscle fiber at the neuromuscular junction, packed with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
A malignant fat-cell tumor with a mucoid matrix and chicken-wire capillaries, usually in the thigh. Caused by the t(12;16) translocation producing a FUS-DDIT3 fusion.
A malignant tumor of fat cells (lipoblasts), typically in the retroperitoneum or thigh of adults. Well-differentiated forms involve MDM2 amplification.
A genus of anaerobic gram-positive rods in skin flora. Cutibacterium (formerly Propionibacterium) acnes contributes to acne and causes infections of prosthetic joints and shunts.

Toxicity from arsenic (contaminated water, pesticides), causing garlic breath, vomiting, diarrhea, Mees lines, peripheral neuropathy and QT prolongation. Chronic exposure raises risk of skin, lung and bladder cancer.
A serine-threonine kinase in the MAPK signaling pathway. Activating V600E mutations occur in melanoma, hairy cell leukemia, papillary thyroid cancer and colorectal cancer; vemurafenib inhibits it.
A reversible P2Y12 platelet inhibitor used after acute coronary syndrome. Causes bleeding and dyspnea.
An irreversible P2Y12 platelet inhibitor used after acute coronary syndrome and stenting; contraindicated after stroke or TIA because of bleeding risk.
A monoclonal antibody that blocks the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor, preventing platelet aggregation. Used in percutaneous coronary intervention; risks include bleeding and thrombocytopenia.

The only laryngeal muscle supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; it tenses the vocal folds to raise pitch. Other laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Inflammation of lymphatic vessels, usually from group A streptococcal or staphylococcal skin infection, producing red streaks extending toward regional nodes.
Pneumonia acquired 48 hours or more after hospital admission, often caused by Pseudomonas, S. aureus (including MRSA) and gram-negative enterics.
A trial design in which each participant receives both the treatment and the control in sequence, serving as their own control, usually with a washout period between them.

A vasodilator that opens potassium channels in arteriolar smooth muscle. Used orally for resistant hypertension and topically for hair loss; causes hypertrichosis, reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.
Recombinant erythropoietin that stimulates red cell production; used in anemia of chronic kidney disease and chemotherapy. Raises thrombosis risk.
Congenital malformations of the skull and face, such as cleft lip and palate, craniosynostosis and micrognathia.
A toxin in pufferfish that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, causing numbness, paralysis and respiratory failure.
The carpal bone at the base of the thumb that articulates with the first metacarpal; a common site of thumb osteoarthritis.
Eye disease in Graves disease from autoantibody-driven inflammation and glycosaminoglycan buildup in orbital tissue, causing proptosis, lid retraction and diplopia.
Infection at the operative wound within 30 days of surgery, most often from S. aureus. Presents with wound erythema, drainage and fever.
A sinus or abscess in the natal cleft over the sacrococcygeal area, thought to result from ingrown hairs, common in young men who sit for long periods.
Impaired bile flow from obstruction outside the liver (gallstone, pancreatic cancer, stricture), causing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, pruritus, pale stool and elevated alkaline phosphatase.
A proteasome inhibitor used in multiple myeloma. Blocking degradation of regulatory proteins triggers apoptosis; causes peripheral neuropathy.
Proteins such as BAX, BAK, BAD and caspases that drive programmed cell death, opposed by BCL-2 and BCL-xL.
An inhibitory receptor on activated T cells that binds PD-L1 on tumor cells, dampening T-cell attack. Blocked by pembrolizumab and nivolumab in checkpoint inhibitor therapy.
A toxic aldehyde formed when cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide are metabolized; it injures the bladder lining, causing hemorrhagic cystitis, prevented with mesna.
A thiol drug that binds acrolein in the urinary tract, preventing hemorrhagic cystitis from cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide.
Painful redness, swelling and peeling of the palms and soles, a side effect of chemotherapy such as capecitabine and 5-fluorouracil, or kinase inhibitors.
Fused-ring aromatic compounds from combustion of tobacco, coal and char-grilled food. Metabolized to DNA-binding carcinogens linked to lung, skin and bladder cancer.
Compression of the ulnar nerve at the elbow (cubital tunnel) or wrist (Guyon canal), causing numbness of the ring and little fingers, weak grip and ulnar claw hand.
Insertion of a tube through the urethra into the bladder to drain urine or measure output. A leading cause of hospital-acquired urinary tract infection.
The posterior thigh muscles (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus) that extend the hip and flex the knee, supplied by the tibial portion of the sciatic nerve.
The heel bone, the largest tarsal bone, forming the heel and attaching the Achilles tendon.
Flat foot, a collapsed medial longitudinal arch. Normal in infants; in adults may result from posterior tibial tendon dysfunction.
An antibiotic that inhibits the first step of cell wall synthesis (MurA). A single dose treats uncomplicated cystitis.
Slow-twitch, red fibers rich in mitochondria and myoglobin that use oxidative metabolism, resisting fatigue; used for endurance and posture.
Fast-twitch, white fibers that rely on glycolysis for rapid powerful contraction but tire quickly; type IIa are oxidative-glycolytic and IIb purely glycolytic.
The heart's primary pacemaker in the upper right atrium, with the fastest spontaneous depolarization. Usually supplied by the right coronary artery.
A test where antibodies clump particles or cells carrying the target antigen, producing visible aggregates; used in blood typing and serologic tests like latex agglutination.
An obligate intracellular bacterium causing murine (endemic) typhus, spread by rat fleas; presents with fever and a truncal rash.
A genus of hard ticks, the vectors of Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii) and tularemia.
Athlete's foot, a dermatophyte infection of the foot, causing scaling, maceration between toes or moccasin-type soles. Diagnosed with KOH preparation.
The carbohydrate-rich coat on the outer surface of cell membranes that aids cell recognition and protection; also a bacterial capsule or slime layer.
An antiseptic used for skin preparation and mouthwash, disrupting bacterial cell membranes.
A vaccine made from a single antigen produced by genetically engineered cells, such as hepatitis B surface antigen from yeast or HPV virus-like particles.
The sensory ganglion of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) in Meckel cave, containing the cell bodies of facial sensory neurons; a site of herpes zoster latency.
A mycobacterial cell wall glycolipid (trehalose dimycolate) that makes bacilli grow in serpentine cords and is toxic to mitochondria; helps virulence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
A second-generation cephalosporin with anaerobic coverage (including Bacteroides), used for intra-abdominal and pelvic infections. Can cause a disulfiram-like reaction and hypoprothrombinemia.
Tear of the spleen, usually from blunt abdominal trauma or infectious mononucleosis, causing left upper quadrant pain, Kehr sign and hemorrhagic shock.
Infection acquired in utero from cytomegalovirus, causing microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss, chorioretinitis and hepatosplenomegaly.
Acquired decline in cognition (memory, attention, language), graded as mild or major (dementia). Causes include Alzheimer disease, vascular and Lewy body disease.
A very high-potency topical corticosteroid used for severe dermatoses like psoriasis and lichen sclerosus; can cause skin atrophy.
Inherited dry, scaly skin from filaggrin deficiency, with fish-scale appearance that spares skin folds; associated with atopic dermatitis.
A dehydropeptidase inhibitor given with imipenem to stop its renal breakdown, preventing nephrotoxic metabolites.
A tetracycline antibiotic that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit, used for acne and MRSA; causes tooth discoloration, vestibular toxicity and photosensitivity.
Examination of the retina, optic disc and fundus with an ophthalmoscope; used to find papilledema, diabetic retinopathy and hypertensive changes.
The jaw joint between the mandibular condyle and temporal bone, with an articular disc; dysfunction causes jaw pain and clicking.
Amphetamine-like designer stimulants ("bath salts") that raise dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin, causing agitation, psychosis, tachycardia and hyperthermia.
A phenothiazine dopamine D2 blocker used as an antiemetic and antipsychotic; can cause extrapyramidal effects and QT prolongation.

Heat illness with heavy sweating, weakness, nausea and headache with normal mental status and core temperature below 40 C. Treated with cooling and fluids; heat stroke is distinguished by CNS dysfunction.
A deeper form of impetigo, typically from group A streptococcus, causing ulcerated punched-out lesions with crusts that heal with scarring. Ecthyma gangrenosum is a Pseudomonas lesion.
Infection by Rickettsia species, small obligate intracellular bacteria spread by arthropods (ticks, lice, fleas), typically causing fever, headache and rash; treated with doxycycline.
Infection by Yersinia pestis, transmitted by flea bites from rodents, causing painful lymph node swelling (buboes), or pneumonic plague by inhalation.
A family of enveloped, negative-sense RNA viruses with a fusion protein, including measles, mumps, RSV, parainfluenza and metapneumovirus. Palivizumab targets the RSV F protein.
A viral enzyme that cleaves polyproteins into functional pieces, essential for maturation; HIV and hepatitis C protease inhibitors block it.
An HIV protease inhibitor that causes nephrolithiasis and hyperbilirubinemia.
A nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor used in HIV treatment and preexposure prophylaxis, usually combined with tenofovir.
An HIV protease inhibitor that strongly inhibits cytochrome P450 3A4, so low doses are used to boost other antiretrovirals.
A bacterial precursor of folate, which sulfonamides mimic competitively; also found in some sunscreens.

A syndrome of marked motor abnormalities, including stupor, mutism, rigidity, posturing, waxy flexibility and excitement. Seen in schizophrenia, mood disorders and medical illness; treated with benzodiazepines.
Surgical excision of skin cancer in thin layers, with each layer microscopically examined until margins are clear. Used for basal and squamous cell carcinoma on the face.
A cytoprotective agent that scavenges free radicals, used to reduce cisplatin nephrotoxicity and radiation-induced xerostomia.
A 30-carbon intermediate in cholesterol synthesis, made from farnesyl pyrophosphate and cyclized to lanosterol.
Antifungals (amphotericin B, nystatin) that bind ergosterol in fungal membranes, forming pores and causing leakage.
Candida bloodstream infection, often related to central venous catheters, IV nutrition or neutropenia. Treated with echinocandins.
An IV artemisinin derivative for severe malaria; produces free radicals that kill Plasmodium in red cells.
An antihelminthic that causes spastic paralysis of worms by activating nicotinic receptors; used for pinworm, roundworm and hookworm.
The pamoate salt of pyrantel, an antihelminthic that depolarizes worm muscle to cause spastic paralysis; used for pinworm and roundworm.
A nematode whose larvae penetrate skin, can autoinfect, and cause chronic disease. In immunosuppressed patients (especially on steroids) it causes hyperinfection; treated with ivermectin.
Infection by Trichinella spiralis from undercooked pork or game, causing periorbital edema, myalgias, fever and eosinophilia as larvae encyst in muscle.

A bedside test of the vestibulo-ocular reflex: a quick head turn with eye refixation saccade means a peripheral lesion, while normal results during acute vertigo suggest a central cause such as stroke.
A topical pyrethroid insecticide that paralyzes arthropods by prolonging sodium channel opening; used for scabies and lice.

Disease from Haemophilus influenzae, an encapsulated gram-negative coccobacillus. Type b causes meningitis, epiglottitis and sepsis in unvaccinated children; nontypeable strains cause otitis media and COPD exacerbations.
Severe leptospirosis with jaundice, kidney failure and bleeding, from Leptospira spread through water contaminated by animal (often rat) urine.
A genus of bacteria without a cell wall, urease-producing, colonizing the genital tract; can cause urethritis and neonatal infection.
A cell wall-lacking, urease-producing bacterium causing nongonococcal urethritis and chorioamnionitis and associated with preterm labor.
The Salk vaccine, an injected killed-virus polio vaccine that induces serum IgG but not mucosal IgA immunity. Replaced the live oral vaccine in the US.
Coxsackievirus A16 infection (also enterovirus 71) causing fever, oral ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles in children.
A genus of tick-borne RNA viruses that includes Colorado tick fever virus, which causes biphasic fever.
An influenza A subtype defined by hemagglutinin 1 and neuraminidase 1 surface proteins, responsible for the 1918 and 2009 pandemics.
A hemorrhagic fever caused by an arenavirus carried by rodents in West Africa, causing fever, mucosal bleeding and hearing loss. Treated with ribavirin.
An oral live vaccine against rotavirus gastroenteritis in infants. Rarely associated with intussusception.
Visualization of the larynx and vocal cords with a scope, used for examination, biopsy and endotracheal intubation.
A topical antibiotic that inhibits bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase; used for impetigo and to eradicate nasal S. aureus carriage.
Inhalation of an object into the airway, most often in young children, causing choking, cough or wheeze. The right main bronchus is the common site in older children and adults.
Immune-mediated loss of Purkinje cells associated with cancer, causing subacute ataxia. Anti-Yo antibodies indicate ovarian or breast cancer; anti-Hu and anti-Tr are other antibodies.
An ATP-dependent drug efflux pump (MDR1) in the gut, kidney, liver and blood-brain barrier; its overexpression in tumors causes multidrug resistance.
A bacterial adaptive immune system using guide RNA to direct Cas9 nuclease to specific DNA sequences; adapted as a gene-editing tool.
An autoimmune skin disease with white, thin, wrinkled vulvar patches causing intense itching and scarring. Increases risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

Life-threatening immune overactivation with uncontrolled macrophage and T-cell activation, causing fever, cytopenias, splenomegaly, high ferritin and hemophagocytosis in marrow. May be inherited or triggered by infection or cancer.
An antimuscarinic drug used to reduce secretions during anesthesia and for drooling or peptic ulcer; does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
Imaging of the bile ducts using contrast, as in ERCP or MRCP, to find stones, strictures and tumors.
An ear-shaped pouch of the atrium; the left atrial appendage is the main site of thrombus formation in atrial fibrillation.
Autosomal recessive DNA helicase (BLM) defect causing excess chromosomal breaks and sister chromatid exchanges, short stature, a sun-sensitive facial rash and high cancer risk.
Glands that secrete products through ducts onto a surface, such as sweat, salivary, mammary and pancreatic glands.
A rare autoimmune blistering disease of pregnancy with IgG against BP180 in the basement membrane, causing intensely itchy urticarial plaques and blisters beginning at the umbilicus.

Dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system, causing orthostatic hypotension, abnormal sweating, gastroparesis and bladder dysfunction. Seen in diabetes, Parkinson disease and Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Surgical cutting or sealing of the vas deferens to prevent sperm entering the ejaculate. Sperm production continues.
Permanent female sterilization by cutting, sealing or removing parts of the fallopian tubes to prevent the egg and sperm from meeting.
Inflammation of the rectal lining, from ulcerative colitis, radiation or sexually transmitted infections (gonorrhea, chlamydia, herpes). Causes tenesmus and rectal bleeding.
The genus of lice that includes Phthirus pubis, the pubic or crab louse.
Inflammation of the pituitary gland causing headache and hypopituitarism. It can be autoimmune or occur with immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration of the pituitary, classically during late pregnancy or postpartum, causing enlargement, headache and hypopituitarism.
Antibodies, usually from horses or sheep, that neutralize venom toxins from snake, spider or scorpion bites.
A surgically created opening between the bowel or urinary tract and the abdominal wall, such as colostomy or ileostomy, for waste drainage.
Waste products that accumulate in kidney failure, such as urea, creatinine, guanidines and middle molecules, causing uremic symptoms like pericarditis, pruritus and encephalopathy.
Recording of muscle electrical activity with needle electrodes to distinguish neuropathic from myopathic disease.
Introduction of gas into a body cavity, such as CO2 into the abdomen during laparoscopy.
A combination bronchodilator of a short-acting beta-2 agonist and a short-acting muscarinic antagonist, used in COPD and acute asthma.
Inflammation of the rectum and colon, such as from ulcerative colitis, infections, or food-protein allergy in infants.
Drugs that block leukotriene effects: montelukast and zafirlukast block the CysLT1 receptor, and zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase. Used in asthma and allergic rhinitis.
Examination of the ear canal and tympanic membrane with an otoscope.
A disorder of compulsive hair pulling causing noticeable hair loss, classified as an obsessive-compulsive related disorder. Treated with habit reversal therapy.
Surgery that routes blood around blocked coronary arteries using grafts such as the internal thoracic artery or saphenous vein.
A semisynthetic opioid agonist used for pain and cough, often combined with acetaminophen.
Chronic watery diarrhea with a normal-looking colon on colonoscopy. Biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltration or a thickened subepithelial collagen band (collagenous colitis).
Pneumonia developing 48 hours or more after endotracheal intubation. Common organisms are Pseudomonas, S. aureus and gram-negative rods.
A fracture in which the overlying skin remains intact, as opposed to an open (compound) fracture.
Degenerative cartilage loss in the knee, causing pain worse with activity, stiffness under 30 minutes, crepitus and joint-space narrowing with osteophytes.
Minimally invasive joint surgery or inspection using a small camera inserted through incisions.
The rim of normal tissue around a resected tumor. A negative margin has no tumor cells at the cut edge; a positive margin does and suggests residual disease.
A Salter-Harris III fracture of the anterolateral distal tibial epiphysis in adolescents whose growth plate is partly closed. Toddler fracture is a spiral tibial shaft fracture in young children.
Protrusion of the rectal wall through the anus, associated with chronic straining, pelvic floor weakness and cystic fibrosis in children.
Weight-loss surgery such as Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy. Can cause deficiencies of iron, B12 and calcium, and dumping syndrome.
A rare gestational trophoblastic tumor from intermediate trophoblasts, producing human placental lactogen with low or modest hCG; resistant to chemotherapy.
Nuclear receptors that bind T3 and act as transcription factors regulating metabolism and development.
A low-risk HPV type (with type 6) that causes genital warts (condyloma acuminata) and laryngeal papillomas; covered by Gardasil.
The HPV vaccine (quadrivalent, later nine-valent) made of recombinant virus-like particles of the L1 capsid protein, protecting against types 6, 11, 16 and 18 (plus others in the nonavalent form).
Infection by Listeria monocytogenes from unpasteurized dairy and deli meat, causing meningitis in neonates and the elderly, and febrile illness and miscarriage in pregnancy.
TB outside the lungs, including lymph nodes (scrofula), spine (Pott disease), meninges, kidney, bone and gastrointestinal tract.
Borrelia infection (louse-borne B. recurrentis or tick-borne) causing recurring episodes of fever from antigenic variation, with Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction on treatment.
The development of detectable antibodies in blood after infection or vaccination.
Surgical replacement or reconstruction of a joint, such as total hip or knee replacement.
An antiparasitic used to treat Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) and, with eflornithine, late sleeping sickness; generates free radicals that damage the parasite.
An osmotic laxative and antacid (milk of magnesia); excess can cause diarrhea and hypermagnesemia in kidney failure.
Maintenance of core body temperature by the hypothalamus through heat production (shivering) and loss (sweating, vasodilation).
Disorder of the inner ear balance organs or nerve, causing vertigo, imbalance and nystagmus; examples include vestibular neuritis and Meniere disease.
A first-generation antihistamine with antimuscarinic effects used for vertigo and motion sickness; causes drowsiness.
An NK1 (substance P) receptor antagonist given for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.
Antiemetics (ondansetron, granisetron) that block serotonin 5-HT3 receptors in the gut and chemoreceptor trigger zone; can prolong the QT interval and cause constipation.
Histamine receptors on gastric parietal cells that stimulate acid secretion through cAMP. Blocked by cimetidine, ranitidine and famotidine.
A proton pump inhibitor that irreversibly blocks the H+/K+ ATPase in gastric parietal cells; used for GERD and ulcers.
An osmotic laxative and bowel prep that retains water in the colon without being absorbed.
A viral enzyme that copies RNA from an RNA template; used by RNA viruses to replicate, and targeted by drugs such as remdesivir.
GTP and GDP, which act as switches for G proteins and signaling; GTP is also an energy source and RNA building block.
A serine-threonine kinase activated by diacylglycerol and calcium after Gq receptor signaling through phospholipase C.
Kinases in a signaling cascade (RAS, RAF, MEK, ERK) that carries growth-factor signals to the nucleus to drive proliferation.
Peptides (ACTH and alpha-, beta-, gamma-MSH) derived from POMC that act on melanocortin receptors to regulate skin pigment, adrenal steroids and appetite.
A receptor on melanocytes activated by alpha-MSH, driving eumelanin production. Loss-of-function variants cause red hair and fair skin.
Elevated 2-hour blood glucose (140 to 199 mg/dL) on an oral glucose tolerance test, short of diabetes; a prediabetes state.
Carrier proteins that bind oxytocin (neurophysin I) and ADH (neurophysin II) during transport down the axons from hypothalamus to posterior pituitary.
An oral vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist that causes free water excretion (aquaresis); used in SIADH and heart failure hyponatremia. Too-rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.
Gq-coupled receptors in the uterus and breast that cause smooth muscle contraction in labor and milk ejection.
A steroid intermediate in the glucocorticoid and sex hormone pathways, made from pregnenolone by 17-alpha-hydroxylase and converted to DHEA.
Anterior pituitary cells that secrete ACTH, derived from POMC; they stain basophilic.
The precursor of insulin made in beta cells; cleavage removes C-peptide, producing insulin. C-peptide level distinguishes endogenous from exogenous insulin.
An IV bisphosphonate that inhibits osteoclasts, used for hypercalcemia of malignancy, Paget disease and bone metastases. Rare osteonecrosis of the jaw.
The pressure needed to stop water moving across a semipermeable membrane toward a solution with higher solute concentration; oncotic pressure from proteins drives capillary fluid balance.
